concepts.title: Sequences and Their Terms
concepts.definition: A sequence is a function whose inputs are the positive integers, so its outputs arrive as an ordered list a_1, a_2, a_3, ... with a clear first term, second term and so on; when the list stops after some term the sequence is finite, and when it runs on forever it is infinite.
concepts.key_idea: Order is the whole point of a sequence: swapping two entries gives a different sequence, unlike an unordered set.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh108.txt lines 20-88 (section 8.2, ordered listing, finite and infinite sequences, population and money examples)
question_patterns: define a sequence and explain how its terms are ordered

solution_steps.explain: A sequence numbers its entries: the image of 1 is the first term, of 2 the second term, and so on, giving a rule or pattern that generates the list.
If the list has a last term it is a finite sequence; if the numbering never ends the sequence is infinite, like the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, ...
In a set the order of elements is irrelevant, but in a sequence rearranging the entries produces a new object.

concepts.title: Series and Summation Notation
concepts.definition: Adding the terms of a sequence one after another produces a series; the Greek capital sigma packs the instruction 'add up all terms of this pattern' into one symbol, with the lower index naming the first term added and the upper index the last.
concepts.key_idea: A series is just a sequence turned into a running total, and sigma notation is the compact grammar for writing that total.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh108.txt lines 89-120 (section 8.3, sigma notation, series corresponding to sequences)

solution_steps.action: Turn the list into an addition
solution_steps.explain: Take the sequence terms and place plus signs between them; the resulting expression is the corresponding series.
The symbol with k running from a lower value to an upper value means: evaluate the general term for each k in range and add all the results.
If k runs from 1 to n the series carries exactly n terms, which matters when matching two ways of writing the same series.

concepts.title: Geometric Progression: One Constant Ratio
concepts.definition: A geometric progression is a sequence in which every term after the first comes from multiplying the previous term by one fixed non-zero number, the common ratio; starting from a first term a the list reads a, a*r, a*r^2, a*r^3 and onward.
concepts.key_idea: Divide any term by the one before it: in a G.P. every such quotient is the same number r, and that single test identifies a G.P.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh108.txt lines 251-355 (section 8.4, definition of G.P., common ratio, example 2, 4, 8, 16, ...)
question_patterns: define a geometric progression and its common ratio

solution_steps.explain: Compute later_term divided by earlier_term for each neighbouring pair of entries in the list.
The list is a geometric progression exactly when every quotient equals one common value r.
With first term a and ratio r the progression runs a, a*r, a*r**2, a*r**3, so the exponent grows by one per step.
Both the first term and the common ratio are kept non zero, otherwise the pattern collapses into a list of zeros.

concepts.title: General Term of a G.P.
concepts.definition: The term sitting in position n of a geometric progression equals the first term times the common ratio raised to the power (n - 1); this single rule generates any term without listing its predecessors.
concepts.key_idea: Position minus one counts how many multiplications by r happened after the first term.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh108.txt lines 356-390 (section 8.4.1 general term of a G.P., a, ar, ar^2, ... pattern)

solution_steps.action: raise the ratio to one less than the position
solution_steps.explain: The first term has no extra factor of r, so the power carried by r in term n is n - 1.

solution_steps.explain: Each step along the progression multiplies by r once more.

concepts.title: Sum of n Terms of a G.P.
concepts.definition: Adding the first n terms of a geometric progression gives a closed result: a times (r^n - 1) over (r - 1) when r differs from 1, and simply n times a when r = 1; for an infinite G.P. with |r| below 1 the sum settles at a / (1 - r).
concepts.key_idea: The subtraction trick: multiplying the partial sum by r shifts it one place, and cancelling the two shifted copies leaves the compact formula.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh108.txt lines 371-460 (section 8.4.2 sum to n terms of a G.P., derivation by subtraction, infinite G.P. sum a/(1-r))

solution_steps.explain: The n-th power of the ratio measures how far the last term has climbed above the first.
One subtracts 1 from the growth factor and scales by the first term.
The denominator is the ratio minus one.
Dividing collapses the n-term addition into one number.

concepts.title: Geometric Mean of Two Positive Numbers
concepts.definition: For two positive numbers a and b, the number that would sit between them in a geometric progression is the square root of their product; between any two positives one can also weave any number of geometric means by choosing a suitable ratio.
concepts.key_idea: The G.M. is the balanced middle under multiplication, exactly as the arithmetic mean is the balanced middle under addition.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh108.txt lines 779-892 (section 8.4.3 geometric mean, G.M. of 2 and 8 is 4, inserting n G.M.s between a and b)

solution_steps.explain: The middle term of a three-term G.P. squares to the product of its neighbours.
Undoing the square gives the geometric mean; positivity of a and b keeps the root real.

concepts.title: Relationship Between A.M. and G.M.
concepts.definition: For any two positive real numbers, their arithmetic mean never falls below their geometric mean, and the two agree only when the numbers themselves are equal; the gap between the two means is (sqrt(a) - sqrt(b))^2 / 2, which is why it can never be negative.
concepts.key_idea: A >= G with equality only at a = b -- a two-number inequality that anchors many maximum and minimum arguments.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh108.txt lines 893-960 (section 8.5 relationship between A.M. and G.M., proof via (sqrt a - sqrt b)^2, example with A = 10, G = 8)
question_patterns: prove that the arithmetic mean of two positive numbers exceeds their geometric mean unless the numbers are equal

in class 11 sequences and series: state the inequality linking A.M. and G.M.
if the A.M. and G.M. of two numbers are given, find the numbers
why can the difference between the two means never be negative
the sum of two numbers and their G.M. are given, determine the numbers

solution_steps.explain: A = (a + b)/2 and G = sqrt(a*b) are the two balanced middles under addition and multiplication.
A - G simplifies to ((sqrt a - sqrt b)^2)/2 once the product is rewritten, and a squared real cannot be negative.
The difference vanishes exactly when sqrt a = sqrt b, that is when a = b; otherwise A stays strictly above G.

solution_steps.action: recover the numbers from A and G
solution_steps.explain: Given A and G, the pair (a, b) are the roots of x^2 - 2A x + G^2 = 0, so two solutions exist (the pair in either order).

concepts.title: Special Series: Sum of the First n Natural Numbers
concepts.definition: Some series repeat so often that their totals deserve memorised formulas; the simplest adds the counting numbers 1 + 2 + ... + n and totals n(n + 1)/2, a result the chapter credits to Aryabhatta alongside the corresponding formulas for sums of squares and cubes.
concepts.key_idea: Pairing the first and last numbers shows why n(n+1)/2 emerges -- every pair contributes the same total.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh108.txt lines 13-19 and 1321-1340 (introduction mentions special series; Aryabhatta note on sums of squares and cubes)
question_patterns: find the sum of the first n natural numbers

in class 11 sequences and series: evaluate the total of the counting numbers up to n

which ancient mathematician is credited with sums of squares and cubes formulas

solution_steps.explain: The product n * (n + 1) counts every paired total twice.
Dividing by 2 corrects the double count and leaves the sum of the first n natural numbers.
